claims.text: The baseline alloy is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The baseline alloy is produced by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering below 1200°C.
Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 has a propensity to form Cr-V-rich precipitates around 8 dpa.
Approximately 5 at.% Hf will be substituted for Cr, producing approximately W38Ta36Cr10V11Hf5.
The proposed irradiation envelope is up to 8 dpa at specimen temperatures no higher than approximately 700°C.
The Hf addition will segregate at grain boundaries and dislocation cores.
Hf is a refractory element with a high melting point.
Minor Hf additions preferentially migrate to defect sites such as grain boundaries and dislocation cores.
Segregated Hf impedes the migration and clustering of Cr and V atoms.
Impeded Cr and V migration and clustering will delay or suppress nucleation of Cr-V-rich precipitates under irradiation.
Suppressing Cr-V-rich precipitation will preserve low hardening and radiation resistance.
The Hf-modified alloy will show minimal or no Cr-V-rich precipitates after irradiation to 8 dpa at temperatures up to approximately 700°C.
The Hf-modified alloy will exhibit hardening similar to or lower than that of the undoped alloy.
Adding Hf while reducing Cr will maintain practical bulk manufacturability.
Cr-V-rich precipitate formation in the baseline alloy is associated with increased hardening.
The baseline alloy has good radiation resistance.
The baseline alloy has good manufacturability.
Sintering above 1200°C, doses above 8 dpa, or irradiation temperatures above approximately 700°C may produce behavior outside the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis repeatedly characterizes the baseline response as low or negligible hardening that should be preserved, whereas the baseline field says Cr-V-rich precipitation is associated with increased hardening.
